summary: Barnaby Teague, the ferry pilot, sits each October dusk on the marsh boardwalk with an empty bamboo cage and counts cricket chirps to learn when the first cold night will come. A retired teacher tells how a traveler from Japan gave him the cage and why he keeps evenings, not crickets.
source_tradition: Japan (the old custom of keeping singing crickets in small bamboo cages) and a common folk rule for reading temperature from cricket chirps
source_note: The cricket-cage custom and the chirp-counting rule are widely known folk practices; the town, characters and story are entirely original.

script:
[[CHAPTER Welcome]]

Welcome to Fernwick Nights. Tonight's story is The Cricket Count, told by Nell Garrity, who spent her life teaching the little ones of Fernwick and now tends the lamps along the marsh boardwalk. Get comfortable, and let the evening settle in around you.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER The Little Cage]]

Walk slowly, there is no rush on this boardwalk. The planks are damp and a little springy, and they give a soft knock under each step. Now, I have a question I have carried for years. Why does Barnaby Teague carry a tiny bamboo cage onto the marsh path every autumn evening, and what lives inside it? He is the ferry pilot, you know, a quiet, weathered man who counts waves in a murmur. Yet each October he comes down here at dusk with a cage no bigger than a teacup, and he sets it on the rail. I asked him once. He only smiled and said, "Come and listen."

[pause]

So I did, and I will tell you what I heard. But first, let me tell you where we are. This is the Salt Marsh path, a long wooden walkway through tall golden reeds, from the last houses of Harbor Lane out to the open sea. It is the middle of October, the last mild week, and the air still holds a little of the day's warmth, like a stone left in the sun.

[pause]

The light is going the color of weak tea. Reeds rustle on both sides with a dry, papery whisper. Small birds are settling into them, one rustle at a time. Far off, the tide laps at the mud with a sound like a cat drinking. The air smells of salt and warm grass and a thread of wood smoke from some chimney back in town.

[long pause]

I should say how I come to be here at all. I taught the youngest children of Fernwick for thirty-eight years, in the brick schoolroom with the crooked clock, and when I stopped, the town gave me a ring of keys and a long taper and a small job. Every evening I light the nine lamps along this boardwalk, one at a time, so that nobody has to walk the marsh in the dark. It takes about half an hour. It is the best half hour of my day.

[pause]

[[CHAPTER Where the Cage Came From]]

Barnaby keeps the cage on a hook by his front door all year, and it is empty. That surprised me. It is made of thin strips of bamboo, tied with fine dark thread, with a little round door the size of a coin and a floor lined with a scrap of green cloth. The bamboo has gone smooth and honey colored from handling. It smells faintly of dry grass.

[pause]

It was a gift. Years ago, a traveler came through on the ferry, a woman named Keiko, from a town in Japan, on her way to see the islands. She sat with Barnaby in the galley for the whole crossing, and she told him something he never forgot. In her country, she said, people have kept singing crickets in small cages for hundreds of years. Not to own them, only to enjoy the song. In autumn, the little bell crickets were sold from carts in the evening streets, and families hung the cages by the window, and a whole house would fall quiet to listen.

[pause]

She said the song was the sound of the turning year. A cricket sings its high, silvery note, and you know that summer has gone and the cool nights are coming. When she left the ferry, she pressed the cage into his hands. "For your listening," she said. And she was gone down the gangway before he could thank her.

[long pause]

Barnaby told me the rest over a cup of strong tea in his galley, with the brown teapot between us and the cracked lid rattling softly as the boat rocked. Keiko had shown him how to tie the thread, and how to cut bamboo so it does not splinter, and how to listen with your whole attention to one small sound. He is not a man who says much. But he said that the crossing felt, afterward, like the quietest hour he had ever spent, and he had spent a good many hours alone on the water.

[pause]

[[CHAPTER The Count]]

Now we have come to the second lamp, and here is the bench where Barnaby sits. I light the lamp each evening with a long taper. It sputters, catches, and settles into a small steady flame behind the glass, with a faint smell of paraffin and warm brass. There. Sit if you like. The boards are still warm.

[pause]

Here is the secret. Barnaby does not keep a cricket in the cage. Not one. He sets the cage open on the rail, with the little door wide, and the crickets of the marsh sing all around it. He listens, and he counts. A field cricket sings faster when the night is warm and slower when it is cool. Count the chirps in fourteen seconds, add forty, and you have nearly the temperature in degrees Fahrenheit. Barnaby learned that from an old almanac in the galley, and he has never found the rule to be wrong.

[pause]

So each evening in October, he sits on this bench with a stub of pencil and a notebook. He counts, and he writes a number. Fifty-nine, he writes, which is a mild night. Then fifty-three, which is a cool one. And the day the number falls below the middle fifties, he knows the first real cold has come. That is the night he lights the galley stove on the ferry for the winter, and brings out the brown teapot, and the whole boat feels like a different place.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER Listening Together]]

Tonight I sat with him. The sky had turned deep blue at the top and pale amber at the edge of the sea. The reeds were dark now, one long soft shape, and the first crickets began. One tiny silver note, then another, then a whole slow chorus, rising and falling like a gentle tide.

[pause]

"Ready?" said Barnaby. He held up his watch. I looked at the second hand as it crept around. He counted in a murmur, one, two, three, with his thumb tapping his knee. The crickets sang at a patient, even pace. When the fourteen seconds were done, he said nineteen, and added forty in his head, and wrote it in the book. Fifty-nine. His pencil scratched softly. He nodded as though a friend had told him good news.

[pause]

The crickets were all around us, though I could not see a single one. They sing from the roots of the reeds, from the cool mud, from under the planks at our feet. Each one makes its note by rubbing one wing against the other, a tiny bow across a tiny string, and the whole marsh hums with it. The sound is neither loud nor soft. It is simply the sound of the evening being exactly what it is.

[pause]

Then he did something I did not expect. He turned the page, and there were all the other years, line upon line of small neat numbers, going back to the autumn Keiko left. Fifty-eight. Sixty-one. Fifty-four. Each one a quiet evening on this same bench. "That is the whole of it," he said. "I never wanted to keep a cricket. I wanted to keep the evenings."

[long pause]

I think that is the loveliest answer I ever heard to anything. We sat there a long while, saying nothing. The lamp glowed beside us, and a moth came to bump gently against the glass, and drifted off again into the dark. Somewhere behind us, the ferry bell rang once, very softly, from the harbor.

[long pause]

There was a pot of tea waiting for us when we got back to the first lamp, left in a quilted cozy on the rail by Ines Larkspur, who sends one down every October evening without being asked. It was still hot. We drank it standing, from two mismatched cups, sweet with a spoonful of honey and smelling of warm leaves. A single cricket sang from the planks by our boots, and Barnaby tilted his head to count it, and then, with a smile, stopped himself and simply listened.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER The Last Warm Night]]

The notebook tells me this is nearly the last of the warm nights. Soon the singing will thin out, one cricket and then two, until the marsh is quiet and the reeds turn silver with frost. Barnaby knows it. He does not mind. He closed the notebook, and slid the pencil into its spine, and rested his hands on his knees.

[pause]

The chorus had slowed a little by then. The notes came farther apart, and each one seemed to hang in the air a moment longer than the last. I felt my own shoulders loosen. The bench, the lamp, the plank under my boots, all of it warm and still.

[long pause]

When at last Barnaby stood, he lifted the little bamboo cage from the rail and held it up to the lamp. The light came through the strips in thin gold lines. He looked inside, at the empty green cloth and the tiny open door. "Plenty of room," he said, with a small smile, "for a good night." Then he hung it on his belt, and we walked back along the boardwalk, slowly, step by quiet step.

[long pause]

The lamps were glowing one after another along the path. The tide was drawing out. The reeds whispered, and the crickets sang on, slower and softer, to the dark and the sea. And nobody was in any hurry at all.

[long pause]

[[SECOND]]

[[CHAPTER Once More, Slowly]]

Why does Barnaby carry a tiny bamboo cage onto the marsh path? Because a traveler gave it to him, and he never put a cricket inside.

[pause]

He sits on the bench by the second lamp. He opens the little door. The crickets sing all around.

[long pause]

He counts the chirps for fourteen seconds. He writes the number in his notebook. A mild night, or a cool one. He keeps the evenings.

[pause]

The lamp glows. The reeds are still. The singing grows slow, and soft, and far apart.

[long pause]

And that is the story of the cricket count. The bench is warm, and the lamp will burn a while yet, and you are welcome to sit with it as long as you like. Good night.
